relationship: God amid a divine assembly
rationale: God stands in an assembly of gods and judges in their midst. Psalm 88 describes God glorified in the council of holy ones and fearsome above those around Him. The assembly surrounding God is a particular shared setting; the gods and holy ones are not thereby assigned an identical human or heavenly identity.

relationship: Impartial judgment against favoritism
rationale: The rebuke asks why the addressees judge injustice and favor sinners. Leviticus forbids injustice in judgment and favoritism toward either a poor person or a ruler, requiring just judgment of a neighbor. Both oppose partial adjudication, while naming different favored groups.

relationship: The earth shaken amid wrongdoing
rationale: The psalm joins lack of understanding and movement in darkness with all the earth's foundations being shaken, following its rebuke of unjust judgment. Isaiah likewise depicts the earth's foundations shaken and the earth falling under the weight of lawlessness. The connection is the disturbance of the earth associated with wrongdoing, without equating the scenes.

relationship: Divine titles confronted with human mortality
rationale: Those addressed as gods in the preceding source unit are told that they die like human beings. Ezekiel challenges Tyre's ruler's claim to be a god when he is a human in the hands of those wounding him. Both juxtapose divine designation and mortal vulnerability, but the psalm's addressed group is not identified with Tyre's ruler or his self-exaltation.

relationship: The uproar of opposition to God
rationale: The psalm describes God's enemies making an uproar and lifting their head. Psalm 2 opens with nations in uproar and rulers gathering against the Lord and His anointed. The noisy opposition to God is a literary parallel, without identifying the unnamed rulers as the coalition listed later in Psalm 82.

relationship: The defeat of Midian recalled in prayer
rationale: The source asks that the present enemies be treated as Midian was. Judges narrates Gideon's companies sounding their trumpets and the Lord setting swords against one another throughout the camp before its flight. The narrated Midian defeat supplies the particular earlier deliverance, without relocating it to the source's separate Kishon example.

relationship: Woodland consumed in divine judgment
rationale: The source uses fire burning a woodland and flame burning mountains before describing God's pursuit of enemies. Isaiah depicts divine judgment as fire consuming the glory of a woodland and leaving few trees. Both use the burning woodland as an image of destructive judgment; their named or unnamed adversaries remain distinct.

relationship: Storm and pursuit in a prayer against enemies
rationale: The source anticipates God pursuing enemies with His storm and troubling them in wrath, following its wind-driven straw image. Psalm 34 asks that enemies become dust before wind while the Lord's angel afflicts and pursues them. The connected wind and pursuit imagery is shared, with God and His angel as the differently expressed agents.

relationship: Enemies brought to shame and trouble
rationale: The prayer asks for enemies' enduring shame and trouble, ending in their perishing. Psalm 6 likewise speaks of enemies being ashamed and greatly troubled, turning back and being ashamed very quickly. The paired reversal is explicit, while the source's duration and destruction are not imposed on the target.

relationship: The heading concerning winepresses
rationale: Both headings say 'For the end' and 'concerning the winepresses.' Psalm 83 attributes its psalm to the sons of Korah, whereas Psalm 8 names David. This is the particular shared heading designation, without assigning it an unstated musical meaning, common author or historical occasion.

relationship: Longing for the living God
rationale: The soul longs for the Lord's courts while heart and flesh exult in the living God. Psalm 41 depicts the soul longing and thirsting for the living God and asking about appearing before His face. Longing for divine presence and the specific designation living God connect the passages.

relationship: Dwelling in God's house and praising Him
rationale: The source blesses those dwelling in God's house and anticipates their enduring praise. Psalm 26 expresses the desire to dwell there throughout life and anticipates sacrifices with shouting, song and music. Both join continued residence at God's house with praise, in a communal blessing and an individual's prayer respectively.

relationship: God appearing in Zion
rationale: The source says the God of gods will appear in Zion. Psalm 101 says the Lord will build Zion and be seen in His glory. The particular divine appearance in Zion connects the promises; the source is not rewritten as worshippers appearing before God.

relationship: The face of God's anointed in prayer
rationale: Psalm 83 asks God to look upon the face of His anointed. Psalm 131 asks Him not to turn away the face of His anointed for David His servant's sake. Both petitions concern God's reception of His anointed's face, without assigning the unnamed anointed in Psalm 83 a historical identity.

relationship: Choosing hardship with God over the pleasures of sin
rationale: The psalmist chooses being cast aside in God's house rather than dwelling in sinners' tents. Hebrews describes Moses choosing mistreatment with God's people rather than temporary enjoyment of sin. The deliberate choice of disadvantaged association with God over sinful comfort is comparable; being cast aside is not changed into a doorkeeper's office.

relationship: Good things not withheld from those devoted to God
rationale: Psalm 83 says God will not deprive those walking in innocence of good things. Psalm 33 says those fearing Him lack nothing and those seeking the Lord will not be deprived of any good thing. The assurance concerning good things is shared, while innocence, fear and seeking remain the passages' respective descriptions.

relationship: A blessing on the person who hopes in the Lord
rationale: The closing verse blesses the person who hopes in the Lord of powers. Jeremiah likewise blesses the person who trusts in the Lord and whose hope the Lord will be. The explicit beatitude and the Lord as the ground of hope supply the correspondence.

relationship: Forgiven lawlessness and covered sins
rationale: Psalm 84 thanks God for forgiving His people's acts of lawlessness and covering all their sins. Psalm 31 blesses those whose lawless deeds were forgiven and whose sins were covered. The paired forgiveness and covering formulation corresponds directly, with communal thanksgiving and beatitude as different forms.

relationship: Divine anger turned away
rationale: Psalm 84 recalls God stopping His wrath and turning away His fury. Isaiah's song thanks the Lord after His anger and says He turned away His wrath and showed mercy. Both describe an experienced reversal of divine anger as grounds for thankful speech.

relationship: God turning back to give life
rationale: The source anticipates God turning back and giving the people life, followed by their rejoicing. Psalm 70 recalls afflictions and God turning back to give the speaker life, then anticipates further comfort. The turning and life-giving action connects communal hope with an individual's recollection and hope.

relationship: Listening for what God speaks within
rationale: The psalmist will hear what the Lord God speaks within him, expecting peace for God's people. Habakkuk stands on his watch to see what God will speak within him and what answer he should give. The distinctive inward-speech expression and attentive posture correspond, without equating the messages or the speakers.

relationship: Lifting the soul toward God
rationale: Psalm 85 asks God to gladden His servant's soul because the speaker lifted it toward Him. Psalm 24 opens by declaring that the speaker lifted his soul to the Lord and hoped in Him. The particular movement of the soul toward God connects the prayers, with gladness requested only in the source.

relationship: The Lord incomparable among gods
rationale: Psalm 85 declares that no one among gods is like the Lord and none of their works is like His. The sea song asks who among gods is like Him and praises His holiness and wonders. The explicit comparison among gods and His incomparable deeds connect the praise without making the psalm a claim to the same occasion.

relationship: The soul rescued from Hades
rationale: Psalm 85 says God's great mercy delivered the speaker's soul from lowest Hades. Psalm 29 thanks the Lord for bringing the soul up from Hades and saving the speaker from descent into a pit. Both attribute the soul's rescue from Hades to God, without identifying the speakers' experiences as the same event.

relationship: Strong adversaries seeking the soul without regard for God
rationale: Psalm 85 says an assembly of strong men sought the speaker's soul and did not set God before them. Psalm 53 likewise describes strong men seeking the soul and not setting God before themselves. The extended hostile description corresponds, while the source's lawless people and the target's strangers remain their respective opening terms.

relationship: The confession of divine compassion and mercy
rationale: Psalm 85 addresses the Lord as compassionate, merciful, long-suffering, abundant in mercy and true. Exodus proclaims the Lord God with the same connected qualities in the encounter with Moses. This sustained description of God's character supplies the link, distinguished from an assertion that the psalm repeats the entire surrounding proclamation.

relationship: The servant who is a maidservant's son
rationale: Psalm 85 asks might and salvation for God's servant, the son of His maidservant. Psalm 115 similarly identifies the speaker as God's servant and His maidservant's son before recalling broken bonds. The distinctive double description connects plea and thanksgiving without establishing that the speakers or mothers are identical.

relationship: Divine comfort and the shame of enemies
rationale: Psalm 85 asks for a good sign and enemies' shame because God helped and comforted the speaker. Psalm 70 anticipates divine comfort and describes those seeking the speaker's harm being ashamed. Comfort and hostile shame are the particular common elements; the target does not expressly supply the requested sign.

relationship: Zion and a register of its people
rationale: The Lord recounts in a register peoples and rulers born in Zion. Hebrews describes approaching Mount Zion and the heavenly Jerusalem, including an assembly of firstborn enrolled in heaven. Zion, belonging and registration connect the images, but the peoples and rulers are not identified as the same registrants as Hebrews's firstborn assembly.

relationship: Dwelling in a city characterized by rejoicing
rationale: Psalm 86 compares dwelling in Zion to that of all who rejoice. Isaiah promises to make Jerusalem an exultation and her people a delight, with rejoicing there replacing weeping. Both characterize the city's life through joy, without replacing the source's dwelling with singers, dancers or springs.

relationship: Crying to God by day and night
rationale: Psalm 87 addresses the God of salvation and describes crying by day and before Him by night. Psalm 21 likewise describes crying by day and night but complains that God will not hear. The paired daily and nightly appeal is shared, while the source's address does not resolve the target's complaint of non-hearing.

relationship: Being counted with those descending into a pit
rationale: Psalm 87 says the speaker was counted with those descending into a pit and became without help. Psalm 27 fears that God's silence will make the speaker like those descending into a pit. The distinctive comparison with the pit's descending company connects a lamented condition with a feared consequence.

relationship: The dead as an image of being forgotten
rationale: Psalm 87 describes wounded people sleeping in a grave whom God remembered no more. Psalm 30 says the speaker was forgotten like a dead person out of mind. The forgotten dead provide the shared image, while God is explicitly addressed as the forgetter only in the source.

relationship: Estrangement from acquaintances and close relations
rationale: Psalm 87 attributes the removal of acquaintances to God and says they made the speaker an abomination. Job describes brothers withdrawing, acquaintances becoming strangers, and relatives, household members and close associates rejecting him. The extended social estrangement is comparable, while the grammatical agency differs and Job's speech is not assigned to the psalmist.

relationship: The dead and the possibility of thanksgiving
rationale: The source asks about wonders for the dead and whether physicians will raise them to give thanks. Hezekiah's prayer contrasts the dead's inability to bless with the living person's blessing of God. The comparison concerns praise from the dead and living; it preserves 'physicians' and does not turn the lament into a comprehensive denial of divine resurrection.

relationship: Divine anger and the sufferers' trouble
rationale: The speaker says God's wraths passed over him and His threats utterly troubled him. Psalm 89 says the community failed in God's anger and was troubled in His fury. The paired divine anger and human trouble are shared, while threats and failure, and singular and communal voices, remain distinct.

relationship: Affliction imagined as engulfing water
rationale: In Psalm 87 the wraths and threats just described encircle the speaker like water and close around him. Psalm 68 cries for rescue as waters enter to the soul, the speaker reaches deep waters and a storm overwhelms him. The surrounding or engulfing water conveys mortal distress, without identifying literal floods or the speakers.

relationship: David and an enduring covenant
rationale: The source records a covenant with God's chosen ones and an oath to David His servant. In David's last words, Samuel records his confidence in God's everlasting covenant with him. The named David and divine covenant make the connection particular, while the source's plural chosen ones is preserved.

relationship: No divine being comparable to the Lord
rationale: The source asks who in clouds or among sons of God can be likened to the Lord. Exodus asks who among gods is like Him, praising His holiness and wonders. The rhetorical assertion of divine incomparability is shared, while clouds, sons of God and gods remain the texts' distinct expressions.

relationship: Divine power defeating enemies
rationale: Psalm 88 describes the arm of God's power scattering enemies, beside the humbling of an unnamed proud one. The sea song praises God's right hand crushing enemies and His greatness shattering opponents. The divine limb and defeated enemies are comparable; the psalm's proud one is not supplied with a name or identified as Pharaoh.

relationship: God's ownership and founding of the world
rationale: Psalm 88 calls heaven, earth and the inhabited world's fullness God's and says He founded them. Psalm 23 likewise declares the earth and its fullness the Lord's and says He founded it. The linked ownership and founding statements form an extended correspondence, with the passages' additional cosmic details kept distinct.

relationship: Mountains personified in exultation
rationale: Psalm 88 names Tabor and Hermon exulting in God's name after mentioning His creation of the north and seas. Psalm 97 summons mountains to exult together, alongside clapping rivers. The mountains' human act of rejoicing is shared, without changing the source's seas into south or identifying the target's unnamed mountains.

relationship: Righteousness and judgment at God's throne
rationale: Psalm 88 names righteousness and judgment as the preparation of God's throne. Psalm 96 uses the same paired qualities as His throne's foundation amid cloud and darkness. The divine throne and its moral basis correspond, while mercy and truth proceeding before God belong to the source's additional clause.

relationship: Joy in God's name
rationale: Psalm 88 anticipates people exulting in God's name throughout the day. Psalm 32 says the community's heart will rejoice in Him because it hoped in His holy name. Both join communal joy with God's name, while the target expressly gives hope as the reason and the source also mentions being raised in righteousness.

relationship: Strength and a horn raised by God
rationale: Psalm 88 names God the boast of the people's power and expects their horn to be raised by His favor. Hannah's song says God gives strength to the kings and will raise the horn of His anointed. The paired divine strength and raised horn are shared, with the community and the expressly royal recipients distinguished.

relationship: David raised from among the people to royal service
rationale: The source recalls a vision in which God raised a chosen one from His people, identified as David in the following unit. Nathan's message recalls God taking His servant David from the sheepfold to lead Israel; its surrounding account calls the message a vision. Both describe David's elevation by God, with the sheepfold detail supplied only by Samuel.

relationship: David's anointing with oil
rationale: The divine speech says God found David His servant and anointed him with holy oil. Samuel narrates the Lord identifying the youngest son and commanding his anointing, then Samuel taking the horn of oil and anointing him. The named David and actual oil-anointing correspond, with God as authorizer and Samuel as executor distinguished.

relationship: Protection from lawless harm in the Davidic promise
rationale: Psalm 88 promises that no son of lawlessness will go on to harm David. Nathan's message promises a place for Israel and says no unjust man will again humble the people. Both belong to promises of protection in the Davidic setting, but the psalm's royal individual and Samuel's people Israel are different recipients.

relationship: God as Father in a royal promise
rationale: Psalm 88 anticipates the king calling God his Father, God and supporter of salvation. Nathan's oracle promises that God will be a father to David's offspring and that the offspring will be His son. The royal father-son relationship is explicit in both, while David's role in the psalm and the promised offspring in Samuel are not collapsed into one immediate addressee.

relationship: An enduring dynasty and throne
rationale: Psalm 88 promises the king's seed for an age of an age and his throne like heaven's days. Samuel promises the house and kingdom made secure for ever and the throne established for ever. The enduring descendants or house and throne correspond, while the heaven-days comparison belongs expressly to the psalm.

relationship: Mercy not withdrawn after royal discipline
rationale: After its threat of discipline, Psalm 88 promises not to scatter mercy away from the king or act unjustly in truth. Samuel likewise follows the disciplinary promise with assurance that God's mercy will not be withdrawn. The conjunction of correction and retained mercy is specific; the target's unnamed removed predecessors are not silently named.

relationship: A plea to remember fragile human existence
rationale: Psalm 88 asks God to remember what the speaker's existence is before questioning whether all humans were created in vain. Job likewise asks God to remember that his life is a breath and speaks of passing good things. Both address human transience to God through a remembrance plea; the psalm's creation question remains a question.
